1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable (cross-sectional survey and qualitative fieldwork in 2016-2017 with no longitudinal follow-up; household recruitment denominators and refusal/nonresponse rates for the N = 258 sample are unreported).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (descriptive/exploratory design with no multivariable statistical adjustment or quasi-experimental control; willingness-to-pay is cross-tabulated solely against an asset-based economic class index without controlling for household size, village infrastructure, distance to water points, or tribal affiliation).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (descriptively maps Kenya's Water Act 2002 regulatory hierarchy—MW&I, WSRB, WSBs, licensed WSPs, bulk-sale contract tariffs of Ksh. 30/m3, progressive domestic block tariffs, and constitutional water rights—and contrasts formal licensing/tariff rules with de facto informal enforcement, but does not systematically audit or code primary licences/contracts at individual sampled standpipes).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern (secondary utility coverage trends rely on WSRB self-reports subject to dormant-connection inflation; primary willingness-to-pay uses spontaneous 4-category responses explicitly noted by the author as potentially unreliable; Table 1 monthly standpipe profit estimates impute a hypothetical 50 L/person/day WHO benchmark rather than measured kiosk sales or household consumption; qualitative FGD/KII instruments and recording protocols are unreported).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Low-to-moderate (captures self-reported retail water prices per litre/jerry can and rich qualitative accounts of queuing, intermittency, and conflict, but does not empirically measure actual household water volume consumed or physical/microbiological water safety, and relies on an unvalidated spontaneous question for willingness-to-pay).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan or protocol; Table 3 reports 0.01 and 0.05 statistical significance asterisks without naming the statistical test or null hypothesis anywhere in the paper; qualitative quotations are illustrative without a documented coding frame or frequency audit).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (purposive single-slum selection of Mathare where >90% use standpipes and water ATMs operate; within Mathare, 258 standpipe-using households were reportedly randomly selected across 13 villages using 2009 census totals, but no 2016-2017 sampling frame, randomisation procedure, or non-standpipe household comparator is provided, and qualitative FGD/KII sample sizes and recruitment criteria are omitted).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The title, abstract, and literature review clearly frame the research question: whether shared paid standpipes can fulfil SDG 6.1 universal access to safe and affordable drinking water for the urban poor in Kenya, examined through national/urban macro coverage trends and micro-level service access in Mathare, Nairobi.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 1 (Title, Abstract) & PDF Page 3 (Literature review, p. 1036)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining WSRB secondary coverage reports with primary structured questionnaires (n = 258 households), focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and field observations in Mathare directly addresses the gap between nominal standpipe coverage and lived affordability/reliability.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: An in-depth qualitative case study using focus group discussions, key informant interviews with community leaders and utility officials, and direct observation at standpipes is appropriate for uncovering informal governance, cartelisation, arbitrary pricing, and tribal queuing dynamics.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Although FGDs, KIIs, and field observations are named, the paper omits the number of FGDs and KIIs conducted, participant recruitment criteria, interview guides, language/translation handling, and audio-recording or note-taking procedures.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper provides zero description of how qualitative interviews, FGDs, and field notes were coded or analysed to derive themes, leaving it unclear whether findings reflect systematic qualitative analysis or selective illustration.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Materials and methods, p. 1037) & PDF Pages 9-12 (pp. 1042-1045)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Interpretations regarding scarcity-driven price hikes, night-time collection hazards, bulk-vendor queue jumping, SHG rotation disputes, and tribal favouritism are substantiated by direct quotations from both standpipe managers and customers alongside direct field observations and tariff data.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 9-12 (Economic accessibility & Water access from standpipes, pp. 1042-1045)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: Substantive links between the research aims and thematic conclusions are coherent, but the complete absence of reported qualitative sampling numbers and analytic/coding methods prevents verification of methodological coherence across collection and analysis.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Materials and methods, p. 1037) & PDF Pages 9-14 (pp. 1042-1047)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Selecting 258 households across all 13 Mathare villages whose main drinking water source was standpipes directly targets users of paid community standpipes to evaluate standpipe tariffs, operations, and willingness to pay, though restricting to standpipe users precludes direct household-level comparison with non-users.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: While 258 households were reportedly randomly selected across 13 villages based on 2009 census counts (27,812 households), the author provides no explanation of how a random sampling frame was constructed in an informal settlement in 2016-2017, how sample size was determined or allocated across villages, or whether respondent demographics match Mathare's population.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: While asset-index economic classification cites Shaban & Sharma (2007) and unit prices paid are straightforward, willingness to pay was measured only by spontaneous 4-category answers that the author admits can be unreliable and yield extreme values, and Table 1 monthly standpipe revenues/profits rely on an imputed 50 L/person/day WHO norm contradicted by slum consumption figures (<20 L/day) cited earlier in the paper.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: Tables 1 and 3 report complete data for 258 respondents, but the paper never states how many households were approached, refusal or non-contact rates, or household replacement rules during fieldwork.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Descriptive tabulations are clear, but Table 3 attaches 0.01 and 0.05 significance asterisks to individual cell counts/percentages without ever identifying the statistical test used, the null hypothesis tested, or software/procedures in Materials and methods.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Materials and methods, p. 1037) & PDF Page 12 (Table 3, p. 1045)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper explicitly justifies combining macro secondary coverage series with primary household questionnaires, FGDs, KIIs, and field observations to examine both aggregate safe-water coverage claims and micro-level socio-economic realities of paid standpipes.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3-4 (Literature review & Materials and methods, pp. 1036-1037)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Macro WSRB coverage data, structured survey findings on tariffs and willingness-to-pay across economic strata, and qualitative interview/observation accounts are integrated throughout the empirical sections to explain why nominal standpipe access falls short of safe, affordable supply.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The author synthesises regulatory reporting incentives, surveyed monopoly markups (70-94%), asset-stratified inability to pay, and qualitative evidence of water theft, vandalism of water ATMs, and tribal favouritism into coherent policy conclusions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Contradictions between rising official WSRB coverage figures versus independent survey/qualitative evidence of severe slum deprivation, and between standpipe managers' claims of competitive pricing versus surveyed retail price spikes during shortages, are explicitly interrogated.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither empirical component fully satisfies the methodological reporting and validity criteria of its tradition: the qualitative strand lacks sample sizes, recruitment details, and analytic coding transparency, while the quantitative strand lacks sampling-frame and nonresponse documentation, uses an unvalidated spontaneous WTP item, and reports unnamed statistical significance tests.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Sarkar (2019) is a convergent mixed-methods case study combining descriptive analysis of Kenyan national/Nairobi regulatory water coverage statistics (WSRB reports), a structured cross-sectional survey of 258 standpipe-reliant households across all 13 villages in the Mathare informal settlement (2016-2017), and qualitative focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and field observations. Under MMAT (2018) criteria (where overall methodological quality cannot exceed the weakest component), the study demonstrates strong mixed-methods rationale and substantive triangulation—effectively contrasting official WSRB coverage gains and formal Water Act 2002 licensing/tariff rules against lived realities of overcrowded standpipes, 70-94% monopoly retail markups during supply shortages, ATM tank water theft, and tribal queuing favouritism—but exhibits high methodological concern due to critical weaknesses in both underlying empirical strands. Specifically, the quantitative descriptive strand provides no 2016-2017 sampling frame or random selection mechanism for informal-settlement households, omits response rates, imputes monthly kiosk revenues using an unrealistic 50 L/capita/day benchmark, measures willingness to pay via spontaneous categorical responses that the author admits can be unreliable, and reports significance stars in Table 3 without identifying the statistical test. Concurrently, the qualitative strand omits FGD/KII sample sizes, recruitment procedures, data-collection protocols, and any thematic coding or reflexivity account.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (per MMAT 2018 guidance, strong mixed-methods integration [5.1-5.4 Yes] is constrained by serious measurement, statistical reporting, and transparency limitations in both the quantitative descriptive [4.3, 4.5 No; 4.2, 4.4 Can't tell] and qualitative [1.2, 1.3, 1.5 Can't tell] components; 5.5 No)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods case study combining secondary descriptive regulatory data analysis, a cross-sectional descriptive household questionnaire survey (n = 258 standpipe-using households in Mathare, Nairobi), and qualitative focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and field observations
raw_response.where_found_summary: Materials and methods (PDF Pages 3-4, pp. 1036-1037); macro secondary analysis (PDF Pages 4-6, pp. 1037-1039, Fig. 1); legal/institutional framework (PDF Pages 6-8, pp. 1039-1041, Fig. 2); primary survey tables and qualitative findings (PDF Pages 8-12, pp. 1041-1045, Tables 1-3); policy synthesis (PDF Pages 13-14, pp. 1046-1047).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study collects, analyses, and integrates both primary quantitative descriptive survey data (structured questionnaire of 258 households in Mathare stratified by an asset-based economic index, reported in Tables 1 and 3 alongside secondary WSRB trend data) and primary qualitative data (focus group discussions, key informant interviews with community leaders and utility officials, and field observations). MMAT (2018) with the Quantitative Descriptive (4.1-4.5) block is therefore the exact matching instrument.
